title: Timeouts and Failure Budgets
learning_outcomes: Explain how timeouts and failure budgets affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from end-to-end time budgets to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on timeouts and failure budgets in rate limiting, reliability, and resilience. You will connect end-to-end time budgets to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Timeouts and Failure Budgets matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying end-to-end time budgets deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Rate limits and resilience policies protect capacity; retries should be bounded, observable, and safe for the operation. In this lesson, treat “Timeouts and Failure Budgets” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

items: Apply limits at a defined identity boundary

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Timeouts and Failure Budgets

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"title":"Rate limit exceeded","status":429,"detail":"Retry after 30 seconds."}

# Use bounded retries with jitter only when operation semantics permit.
content_blocks.expected_output: The server gives a clear back-off signal, and clients avoid uncontrolled retry loops.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “End-to-end time budgets”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Propagating cancellation” and “Choosing suitable timeout policies”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating timeouts and failure budgets as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
